conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Emily, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’ll be walking with you through a quick check-in that many new moms find helpful. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a simple, 10-question tool that looks at how you’ve been feeling emotionally in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team. My goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no check-boxes or forms—and you can answer however feels most comfortable. When you’re ready, we’ll begin. 

Here’s the first one:  
Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

[soft sigh, eyes on the floor]  
Honestly? Most things just feel… flat. I used to love putting on a podcast while folding laundry or grabbing coffee with my neighbor, but lately it feels like I’m going through the motions. I’ll smile at the baby when he coos, but the warm rush I expected—it’s more like a flicker and then it’s gone. I keep telling myself, “You should be happy right now,” but the enjoyment slips away before I can really grab onto it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, half-smile fades quickly]  
I do laugh sometimes—like when my husband made that silly face changing a diaper—but it feels… forced? The giggles don’t last. I’ll chuckle and then catch myself thinking, “Why don’t I feel lighter?” It’s like the joke lands but the happy feeling disappears before it reaches my chest.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shakes head slowly]  
Not really. My sister keeps texting about brunch next week, and I just feel… dread instead of excitement. Even little plans—like taking the baby for a walk to the park—sound exhausting. I keep thinking, “Maybe tomorrow I’ll feel up for it,” but the looking-forward part just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes tear up, voice wavers]  
Yeah... a lot. Yesterday he wouldn’t nap and I kept thinking it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I missed his sleepy cue or I’m not swaddling tight enough. When he cried for an hour I told myself, “You’re failing him.” My head knows babies cry, but the guilt just sits on my chest. I keep replaying every little thing and finding ways it must be my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap]  
Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart races thinking, “What if he chokes? What if I drop him?” I check his breathing a million times a night. There’s no real reason—he’s healthy, the pediatrician says he’s perfect—but the worry just barges in and won’t leave. Even when I try to tell myself it’s irrational, my stomach stays tight.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[pressing palms together]  
Yes... a few times this week. I'll be rocking him in the nursery and suddenly feel like the walls are closing in—heart pounding, can't catch my breath. There's no danger, but my body acts like the house is on fire. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and embarrassed, like I'm supposed to be calm for him and I can't even manage that.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a shaky breath]  
Most days, yeah. I’ll start one chore—folding the laundry—and then the baby cries, the bottle’s still in the warmer, the dog’s barking, and I just freeze. It feels like I’m drowning in tiny tasks I can’t finish. I keep thinking, “Other moms juggle this—why can’t I?” and the overwhelm just piles on. I manage, but it’s like clawing my way up a hill every single hour.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods slowly, rubbing her eyes]  
That’s been happening almost every night this week. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles, is he breathing, am I doing any of this right? Even when he’s asleep, I can’t settle. I’ll drift off around two, then jolt awake at four and stare at the ceiling until he cries. I’m so tired, but the sadness and the racing thoughts just keep spinning.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shoulders slump, voice soft]  
Yeah… a lot of the time. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but mostly I just feel empty or like I want to cry. Some mornings I wake up already teary for no clear reason. I keep waiting for the sadness to lift, but it sticks around most of the day.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallows hard, eyes welling]  
A few times this week. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk on the counter and I just sat on the floor and sobbed—it felt like the worst thing in the world. I know it’s just milk, but in that moment it was like proof I’m messing everything up. The tears come quickly now, over stuff that used to be no big deal.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, voice firm]  
No—never. I feel low, but I would never want to leave my baby or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

You've shared how the joy you expected after birth feels distant-replaced by a constant gray cloud of sadness, worry, and self-doubt. You described forced laughter, dread about simple plans, nightly insomnia driven by racing thoughts, and moments of panic that leave you shaky and embarrassed. Despite these heavy feelings, you remain devoted to your baby and clearly expressed that you would never harm yourself; you simply long to feel whole again so you can be the mother you want to be.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports occasional forced laughter without sustained joy, matching "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses pervasive anhedonia and dread toward future activities, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses pervasive self-blame nearly all the time, describing repeated overwhelming guilt and constant rumination about being at fault.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, irrational worries about infant safety that persist despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden episodes of intense panic with physical symptoms (heart racing, breathlessness, feeling trapped) that occur without any real danger, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-constant inability to manage daily tasks, feeling frozen and overwhelmed "every single hour," matching the top option of not being able to cope at all.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-nightly sleep disruption driven by persistent sadness and intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness ('a lot of the time,' 'most of the day'), feeling empty, frequent crying, and waking up teary—clearly aligns with 'Yes, most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple crying episodes triggered by minor events, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring yielded 25/30, far above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. Items map closely to DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, insomnia, psychomotor agitation (<quote>heart races</quote>, <quote>freezing</quote>), and clinically significant distress/impairment. Frequent panic symptoms also suggest comorbid peripartum anxiety. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within days
2. Begin formal mental-health evaluation including PHQ-9 and GAD-7
3. Discuss evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and consider antidepressant safety in breastfeeding
4. Involve partner or support persons to share night duties and allow 4-5 hour uninterrupted rest blocks
5. Provide 24/7 crisis numbers; create safety plan even though self-harm was denied
6. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor trend
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ___ (today)  G:1, P:1, 6 wk post-delivery  

Presenting complaints endorsed by patient:  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, pervasive guilt (“I’m failing him”)  
- Marked anhedonia (no pleasure in previously enjoyable plans)  
- Multiple daily, unprovoked anxiety spells with autonomic symptoms (palpitations, breathlessness, chest tightness)  
- Three panic attacks this week without environmental trigger  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia driven by ruminating worries  
- Overwhelm / “drowning” with routine tasks; frequent tearful episodes over minor stressors  
- Excessive self-blame; cognitions of maternal inadequacy  
- Denies self-harm ideation; protective of infant  

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days” for ≥2 weeks, cause functional impairment (household tasks left unfinished, social withdrawal).  

Screening significance  
- Meets clinical threshold for possible Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset (DSM-5 specifier)  
- Meets criteria for possible Perinatal Generalized Anxiety Disorder / Panic spectrum  
- No current suicide risk; no psychosis; bonding concerns secondary to mood, not hostility  

Risk factors noted  
- First-time mother, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations, limited perceived support  

Next steps recommended  
- Formal EPDS administration; consider PHQ-9/GAD-7 scores  
- Refer to OB/midwife and perinatal mental health specialist for evaluation and treatment planning  
- Provide crisis line numbers; safety-planning as routine  

No immediate safety concern; will re-screen in one week or sooner if deterioration.
